newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Alcoa China alumina deal a shrewd move.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Alcoa China alumina deal a shrewd move.

text.p: Alcoa's 30-year deal to sell alumina to China was a shrewd move to lock in output from its planned Wagerup expansion, and take a lucrative slice of the spot market from under traders' feet, industry sources said.
But some warn the world's biggest aluminum group may be prey to China's habit of "price majeure" - insistence on renegotiating tags if markets tumbled after the ink dried on sales contracts.
The alumina will be supplied by Alcoa's 60 percent owned Alcoa World Alumina and Chemicals. WMC Ltd of Australia has the remaining 40 percent stake.
Some two tonnes of alumina is used for each tonne of aluminum.

Traders said news of the deal has been rippling through the market for several weeks, with Monday's announcement carefully leaving out key details of how much China pays for the 400,000 tonnes a year it agreed to buy.
"The information that we hear is there is a nominal base price of $140 per tonne," an alumina trader said.
He estimated that with interest at 6.5 percent translating into $8 million a year on 400,000 tonnes, the overall alumina price would be about $200 per tonne.
"That's a very good deal for Alcoa whose cash costs are less than $100 per tonne," the trader said.
An analyst said he "heard whispers" the price was based on cost plus freight or about $120 per tonne, rather than market prices, now about $155 on spot basis.
However, one source believed there may be an Australian government ruling that alumina can only be exported at market and not cost price. Others disputed this.
China usually buys alumina on a spot basis or on contracts lasting a year or so. Traders take a healthy slice of the business.
"This deal will give Alcoa a base load and it will take some of the traders out of business," a merchant suggested.
"It's quite surprising," said analyst Tim Armstrong of CRU International. "Extremely long-term deals in China are something of a rarity."
Alumina sources said the deal boiled down to how confident Alcoa was of getting the contract to perform, though many believed the deal was simply formalizing the company's spot business with China.

But one European analyst said the key to the deal was China's thirst for alumina and Alcoa's wish to expand production. "It's clear that the Chinese have been interested in getting some share in Western alumina refining. China has aluminum smelter expansions and will continue to be short of alumina."
Alcoa is mulling a A$950 expansion of its Wagerup alumina refinery in Western Australia to 3.3 million tonnes a year.
"I would say this deal has to be tied to the Wagerup expansion," the European analyst said.

The China deal will guarantee a market for the additional alumina from Wagerup, and nip in the bud the risk of the Chinese going elsewhere to secure the long-term supplies they badly need, analysts said.
Alcoa spokeswoman Bonnie Cersosimo said the Wagerup expansion plan was still on hold. The decision to move ahead will be based on overall bookings and market, not just on one specific deal.

"This is not an equity deal - it's a commercial deal for the long-term sale of alumina," Cersosimo said, adding that Alcoa was not reciprocating by taking an equity stake in any Chinese aluminum smelter.

Cersosimo said Alcoa is producing alumina at the rate of 10.5 million tonnes a year, with a further 350,000 tonnes of capacity at operating plants curtailed. In addition, the start-up of completed brownfield expansions at Sao Luis, Brazil, and Point Comfort in Texas was still on hold.
A further 600,000 tonnes of capacity is also shuttered at the company's St Croix refinery.
"That is an awful lot of capacity," a New York stock analyst said. "I don't think they would make an announcement about Wagerup until some of that has been restarted or more fully utilized."
Nevertheless industry sources noted that Australia, not the Americas, was the natural alumina supplier to China because of cheaper freight costs.
Many of the aluminum smelter expansions due on stream between now and 1998 will also be looking to Australia for their alumina, traders noted.
